exercise.text_title: The Volunteer Job I Chose for the Wrong Reason
exercise.article:
When I first signed up to volunteer at a community repair workshop, my motivation was anything but noble. I had heard that volunteering looked impressive on university applications and CVs, and I thought it might give me an edge in the competitive job market. I imagined myself learning practical skills, fixing broken appliances, and perhaps even making some useful connections. However, my experience turned out to be quite different from what I had expected.

On my first day, I arrived with a sense of anticipation, ready to dive into the world of repairs. To my surprise, instead of being handed a toolbox, I was asked to greet visitors and find out what help they needed. Initially, I was disappointed; this wasn't what I had signed up for. I had pictured myself as a hands-on problem solver, not a receptionist.

It wasn't long before a visitor arrived, looking sheepish and holding a toaster. As I approached, he admitted he felt embarrassed for not knowing how to fix it himself. I realised that my role was not just about directing people to the right volunteer but also about making them feel comfortable. I found myself explaining the repair process in simple terms, ensuring he didn't feel foolish. This interaction taught me the importance of patience and empathy, skills I hadn't anticipated developing in this environment.

As the weeks went by, I began to enjoy coordinating tasks among volunteers with different skills. I discovered a knack for organising people and resources, ensuring that each visitor received the help they needed. This was a far cry from the practical repair work I had envisioned, but I found it surprisingly fulfilling.

Eventually, it was time to update my CV, and I realised that the most significant outcome of my volunteering wasn't a new line about technical skills. Instead, it was a changed perspective on what I valued in a job. I had always assumed that career satisfaction came from mastering a specific skill, but my time at the workshop taught me that I enjoyed roles involving people-facing coordination more than I had ever expected.

Reflecting on my initial reasons for volunteering, I can't help but smile at how misguided I was. While the experience did enhance my CV, the true value lay in the personal insight I gained. I now know that the work I find most rewarding involves not just technical tasks but also meaningful interactions with others.
